notes:
Now let me check a couple more important sources from the search results I received.

Here are the verse-by-verse notes for **Numbers 22:1–20**, drawn from the approved sites.

---

## v. 1 — “Then the Israelites traveled on and camped in the plains of Moab near the Jordan, across from Jericho.”

**Geographical setting.** This verse marks Israel’s arrival at the staging ground for the conquest of Canaan. They had finished their 38-year wilderness exile and were now poised east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho. They would remain in this general area for about a year, through the end of Deuteronomy and into Joshua. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

The “plains of Moab” had formerly belonged to Moab but had been wrested from them by Sihon the Amorite, and then taken from Sihon by Israel. The site is a dry, sunken desert region in the Jordan Valley, a little north of the Dead Sea. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/22.htm — Jamieson-Fausset-Brown; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-22-commentary — Wenham)

Israel’s victories over the southern Canaanites, the Amorites under Sihon, and Og of Bashan (Numbers 21) had prepared this new generation for the battles ahead. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

The Hebrew verb for “journeyed” (*nasa‘*) means “to pull up tent pegs,” a technical term for breaking camp — used over 100 times in Numbers, picturing Israel as desert travellers folding tents and moving on. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-22-commentary)

---

## v. 2 — “Now Balak son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites.”

The name **Balak** means “devastator,” “waster,” or “swallower of the people.” According to Fausset’s Bible Dictionary, Balak was not a hereditary king but had been imposed on Moab by Sihon the Amorite. His knowledge of a seer living as far away as Mesopotamia (Balaam) implies a surprising circulation of intelligence in that era, likely aided by merchant caravans and Moab’s relatively advanced civilization (later evidenced by the Moabite Stone). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-22-commentary — Fausset)

Balak had witnessed the destruction of the powerful Amorites — a nation stronger than Moab — and understood that militarily he was no match for Israel. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-22-commentary)

---

## v. 3 — “and Moab was terrified of the people because they were numerous. Indeed, Moab dreaded the Israelites.”

The Hebrew verb translated “dreaded” (*quts*) denotes loathing, being sickened, or feeling revulsion. It describes deep emotional reaction that issues in desired repulsion of the object abhorred. The Septuagint uses *prosochthizō*, the same verb describing Yahweh’s reaction to Israel in Hebrews 3:10, 17. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-22-commentary)

Matthew Henry notes the irony: the Moabites needed not fear Israel because God had commanded Israel not to harass Moab (Deuteronomy 2:9). “Thus were the wicked in great fear where no fear was” (Psalm 53:5). If they had known and believed God’s word, they would have had nothing to fear. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html)

Rabbi Hirsch explains that the verb used for “dread” (*quts*) can provoke such violent emotion that it might make one vomit. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/ — citing Allen)

---

## v. 4 — “So the Moabites said to the elders of Midian, ‘This horde will devour everything around us, as an ox licks up the grass of the field.’ Since Balak son of Zippor was king of Moab at that time…”

**Alliance with Midian.** The Moabites enlisted the elders of Midian to form a coalition. This alliance is significant because Midianite women later feature in the seduction of Israel at Baal-Peor (Numbers 25:6–9). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

**The ox metaphor.** The proverbial figure of an ox licking grass is “particularly fitting for a pastoral people” and serves as “an emphatic symbol of her strength and power.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/ — citing Allen)

**Economic, not military fear?** Bible.org’s commentator (Bob Deffinbaugh) argues that the Moabites’ real fear was economic rather than military: “Now this mass of people will lick up everything around us, as the bull devours the grass of the field” suggests they feared Israel would consume the natural resources, leaving too little for Moab — much like the strife between the herdsmen of Abraham and Lot (Genesis 13:5–7). They did not mention slaughter, only being “devoured” economically. (https://bible.org/seriespage/balaam-part-i-numbers-221-35)

Matthew Henry points out that the Moabites, had they pleased, could have made good use of Israel’s advances: they should have rejoiced that Israel freed them from the threatening power of Sihon, who had taken part of their land. Instead, having forsaken the religion of their father Lot and sunk into idolatry, they hated the people of the God of Abraham. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html)

---

## vv. 5–6 — “he sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor at Pethor, which is by the Euphrates in the land of his people…”

**Who was Balaam?** Balaam suddenly appears in the narrative. He was from Pethor (ancient Pitru) near the Euphrates, about 400 miles from Moab — a journey of 20–25 days. The 1967 discovery of the **Deir ‘Alla Inscription** in Jordan, dated between the 9th century BC and the Persian period, mentions “Balaam son of Beor” as a seer who specialized in curses and received revelation by night. The inscription and the Numbers account show striking correspondences: both depict Balaam as a diviner/seer (not a Hebrew prophet), both use divine names similarly (including *Shaddai*), and in both Balaam receives revelation at night. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-22-commentary; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

Balaam was “not a good prophet who went bad or a bad prophet trying to be good. He is altogether outside Israel’s prophetic tradition. He is a pagan, foreign national whose mantic acts center on animal divination.” He “believed that he had a way with the gods, a hold on them. To him Yahweh was not the Lord of heaven but just another deity whom he might manipulate.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/ — citing Allen)

Yet Balaam did have some knowledge of the true God, similar to Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18) and Jethro (Exodus 18) — non-Israelites who came to know the true God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

**The request to curse.** Balak wanted Balaam to curse Israel to cripple them spiritually so they could be defeated in battle. Balak recognized that Israel’s strength was spiritually rooted. As far as Balak was concerned, Balaam’s blessing or curse determined a nation’s fate — language that “immediately brings to mind the words of the Abrahamic Covenant” (Genesis 12:3). Ironically, Balak’s plan to curse Israel was destined to bring a curse upon himself. (https://bible.org/seriespage/balaam-part-i-numbers-221-35)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that forty years had passed since Israel left Egypt, yet Balak’s words “a people has come out of Egypt” expressed a great truth: Israel was still the same organized nation that had spoiled Egypt. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/22.htm)

---

## vv. 7–8 — “The elders of Moab and Midian departed with the fees for divination in hand… ‘Spend the night here,’ Balaam replied, ‘and I will give you the answer that the LORD speaks to me.’”

**“Fees for divination.”** This was a transactional, pagan approach to spiritual matters — paying for supernatural favour. Scripture records this practice as morally corrupt (Ezekiel 13:19; Micah 3:11). True prophecy is never for sale (2 Kings 5:15–16; Acts 8:18–20). Balaam’s later condemnation as one “who loved the wages of wickedness” (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11) roots back to this moment. (https://biblehub.com/q/What_does_Numbers_22_7_mean.htm)

Adam Clarke notes that whoever consulted a prophet took a present, but here “more than a mere present is intended, perhaps every thing necessary to provide materials for the incantation. The drugs, &c., used on such occasions were often very expensive.” Balaam “was very covetous, and…loved the wages of unrighteousness.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/ — citing Clarke)

**Balaam’s initial response.** Balaam invited the men to stay overnight so he could hear from God. But it was “clearly wrong — then and now — to be a prophet for hire.” He was “seeking God’s will” regarding something that was plainly not His will. Immediately his heart was revealed: though he had significant spiritual gifts, he was not a man with a genuine heart after God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

Matthew Henry comments: “When we enter into a parley with temptations we are in great danger of being overcome by them.” Balaam “lodges the messengers, and takes a night’s time to consider what he shall do” — he should have given his answer immediately. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html)

Balaam’s use of “the LORD” (Yahweh) is striking — he used the covenant name of Israel’s God, which betrays that he knew more than his visitors had told him. (https://bible.org/seriespage/balaam-part-i-numbers-221-35)

---

## vv. 9–11 — “Then God came to Balaam and asked, ‘Who are these men with you?’ … Balaam said to God, ‘Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent me this message…’”

**God’s question.** God knew the answer, but asked because Balaam did not truly know who these men were — they were evil men on an evil errand, and Balaam did not act accordingly. As parents ask children questions to which they already know the answer, God was probing Balaam’s heart. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/; https://bible.org/seriespage/balaam-part-i-numbers-221-35)

**God “came to” Balaam.** The expression “God came to” (Hebrew) does not suggest God came in response to Balaam’s efforts to contact Him. Its other uses (Genesis 20:3 to Abimelech; Genesis 31:24 to Laban) indicate God came unexpectedly, probably in a dream, to pagans — not as a reward but as a sovereign intrusion. (https://bible.org/seriespage/balaam-part-i-numbers-221-35)

**Balaam’s report.** Balaam gave a truthful but incomplete report, omitting Balak’s extravagant claim that Balaam’s blessing or curse determined fate. He simplified: “come and put a curse on them for me.” (https://bible.org/seriespage/balaam-part-i-numbers-221-35)

---

## v. 12 — “But God said to Balaam, ‘Do not go with them. You are not to curse this people, for they are blessed.’”

**God’s clear prohibition.** God’s word was unambiguous — two commands and a reason: do not go, do not curse, for they are blessed. The blessing refers back to Genesis 12:3 (“I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse”) and to Jacob’s irreversible blessing by Isaac (Genesis 27:33). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/22.htm)

Gill notes that God “had no obligation to respond to a greedy, self-seeking heart like Balaam’s. But in mercy God did respond, warning Balaam to have nothing to do with these men.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/22.htm — cited via Enduring Word)

Matthew Henry adds: “Israel had often provoked God in the wilderness, yet he will not suffer their enemies to curse them, for he rewards them not according to their iniquities. The blessedness of those whose sin is covered comes upon them” (Romans 4:6–7). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html)

Maclaren notes that, though forbidden to curse in words, Balaam later “did it in another way — by means of Baal-peor” (Numbers 25; Revelation 2:14). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/ — citing Maclaren)

---

## vv. 13–14 — “So Balaam got up the next morning and said to Balak’s princes, ‘Go back to your homeland, because the LORD has refused to let me go with you.’ … And the princes of Moab arose, returned to Balak, and said, ‘Balaam refused to come with us.’”

**Balaam’s partial report.** Balaam told the messengers only that the LORD refused him permission to go. He “did not tell them, as he ought to have done, that Israel was a blessed people, and must by no means be cursed; for then the design would have been crushed, and the temptation would not have been renewed.” Instead, “he, in effect, desired them to give his humble service to Balak, and let him know that he applauded his project, and would have been very glad to gratify him.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html)

The Geneva Study Bible comments: “Or else he would have been willing, covetousness had so blinded his heart.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/numbers-22.html)

**The messengers’ partial report.** They said only “Balaam refused to come with us,” intimating he merely wanted more courtship and higher offers. “Thus are great men wretchedly abused by the flatteries of those about them, who do all they can to prevent their seeing their own faults and follies.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html)

Balaam’s message effectively communicated: “God told me no, but perhaps you can persuade me.” King Balak understood perfectly. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

---

## vv. 15–17 — “Then Balak sent other princes, more numerous and more distinguished… ‘Please let nothing hinder you from coming to me, for I will honor you richly and do whatever you say.’”

**The escalated temptation.** The second embassy was “more, and more honourable.” No longer just the diviner’s fee — now Balak promised “very great honour” and a blank cheque: “I will do whatever you say.” Balak appealed to both covetousness and pride. Matthew Henry reflects: “How earnestly should we beg of God daily to mortify in us these two limbs of the old man!” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html)

**“Let nothing hinder you”** — in essence, Balak told Balaam not to let the clear commands of Yahweh prevent him from coming. This is direct defiance of divine directives. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-22-commentary)

Because Balaam had refused to decisively put away the temptation the first time, “now the temptation came back to him stronger than it was before.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

---

## vv. 18–19 — “But Balaam replied… ‘If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not do anything small or great to go beyond the command of the LORD my God. So now, please stay here overnight as the others did, that I may find out what else the LORD has to tell me.’”

**Good words, corrupt heart.** Balaam’s words sound noble: he calls God “the LORD my God,” speaks respectfully of God’s word, and seems to disdain wealth. Yet “the searcher of hearts knew that he loved the wages of unrighteousness. It is an easy thing for bad men to speak very good words, and with their mouth to make a show of piety. There is no judging of men by their words. God knows the heart.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html)

**Naming his price.** With a tone of longing, Balaam effectively suggested a bigger offer. Constable notes: “He would not go for a large sum, but when his visitors offered a sum larger than what he had mentioned would be inadequate, he reconsidered.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-22.html — cited in search results)

**“What more the LORD will say.”** These words sound spiritual but were not. God had already clearly spoken. Balaam “was like a child who, having once heard the father’s answer, will ask again, hoping the father’s will might change.” It was “a vile reflection upon God Almighty, as if he could change his mind…Surely he thought God altogether such a one as himself.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

The Geneva Study Bible on v. 19: “Because he tempted God to require him contrary to his commandment, his petition was granted, but it turned to his own condemnation.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/numbers-22.html)

---

## v. 20 — “That night God came to Balaam and said, ‘Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them, but you must only do what I tell you.’”

**The most debated verse in the passage.** God appears to reverse His earlier command. The central question: did God change His mind, or was this permission actually a form of judgment?

**Traditional Protestant consensus — God’s permissive will as judgment:**

- **Matthew Henry:** “God gave him up to his own heart’s lust. ‘Since thou hast such a mind to go, even go’…It was in anger that God said to Balaam, ‘Go with them.’ … As God sometimes denies the prayers of his people in love, so sometimes he grants the desires of the wicked in wrath.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-22.html)

- **Enduring Word (Guzik, Pentecostal/Charismatic):** “God did not change His mind. Balaam would not now be in the will of God if he went with Balak’s messengers…God’s permission to go was actually an act of judgment, similar to Jesus telling Judas to do what he was planning to do (John 13:27).” G. Campbell Morgan: “He was first forbidden, and afterwards commanded to go. The only explanation that is satisfactory is that, while attempting to maintain an external obedience to this supreme will of God, his heart was lusting after the riches offered to him by Balak.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-22/)

- **Dr. Constable (Evangelical/DTS):** “Numbers 22:12 contains the directive will of God and Numbers 22:20 the permissive will of God. The change was due to God’s yielding to Balaam’s desire…The permission of Numbers 22:20 constituted a test for Balaam, which he failed. Balaam knew the will of God (Numbers 22:12), but God gave him permission to obey or disobey (Numbers 22:20).” (from search results)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** “This event illustrates the two aspects of the will of God: (1) direct, and (2) permissive. He may allow what He does not endorse…God may allow His child to follow a course of action that He disapproves, but He uses this as a means of judgment upon the disobedient spirit.” (from search results)

- **Gill (Reformed Baptist):** The permission “was not a command, but a concession, or rather a permission, leaving him to go if he would, suffering him to follow his own heart’s lusts, and giving him up to them to his own destruction.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/22.htm)

- **Geneva Study Bible (Reformed):** God “warned him by a dream, that he should not consent to the kings wicked request” (v. 12). The later permission was God yielding to Balaam’s persistent covetousness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/numbers-22.html)

- **Pulpit Commentary Homiletics:** “We must look not only at the letter of God’s commands, but the spirit of them…The obedient heart will distinguish between the permissive and the imperative, between the concession to human weakness and the call to holy duty. Those who want to be right with God…will never lift a permission into a command. Our interpretations of God’s words are a searching test of our spiritual state.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/22.htm)

- **Robert A. Watson (Expositor's Bible):** Balaam “receives it, but with a reservation…In repeating his inquiry he has assumed that the God of Israel is amenable to human urgency; and as he will have Jehovah to be, so within limits he seems to find Him.” (https://ccel.org/ccel/watson_ra/expositornum/expositornum.xx.html)

**Summary of differences between traditions:**

The basic interpretation that God’s permission was a judgment on Balaam’s greed is shared across **all Protestant traditions surveyed** — Baptist (Garner-Howes, Gill), Reformed/Puritan (Matthew Henry, Geneva Bible), Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word), and Evangelical (Constable, Bible.org). The differences are mainly ones of emphasis:

- **Reformed** teachers stress God’s sovereignty in giving Balaam over to his sin as an act of judicial hardening.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** teachers (Guzik) stress the spiritual blindness and the principle that seeking God’s permission for what He has already forbidden invites judgment.
- **Baptist** teachers (Garner-Howes) stress that Balaam was not truly saved — his faith was “from the head, not from the heart.”
- **Evangelical** teachers (Constable, Bible.org) emphasize the distinction between God’s “directive” and “permissive” will as a test Balaam failed.

**Catholic reading:** I was unable to fetch specific Catholic/Orthodox pages due to tool limits. The search did retrieve a reference to the Catholic Haydock Commentary, but the page could not be loaded for detailed notes.

**Modern scholarship:** The **NET Bible notes** (cited at Precept Austin) divide the chapter structurally into four sections: invitation declined (vv. 1–14), second invitation extended (vv. 15–21), God opposes Balaam (vv. 22–35), and Balaam meets Balak (vv. 36–41). The **Deir ‘Alla inscription** (discovered 1967) confirms Balaam was a known historical/literary figure in the Transjordan, a pagan seer who received revelation at night, consistent with the biblical portrait. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-22-commentary)

**“Only do what I tell you.”** God’s one absolute reservation was that Balaam could speak only what God allowed. This “is the point of the whole chapter: Balaam the pagan mantic will not be able to speak cursing as he had planned. Instead, he would be the most surprised of all; he would be the most remarkable instrument of God in the blessing of his people, Israel” (Allen, cited in Constable). (from search results)

---

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

| Theme | Consensus |
|---|---|
| Balaam’s identity | A pagan diviner, not a true prophet of Yahweh, though he knew the name “Yahweh” and God spoke to him sovereignly |
| Balaam’s sin | Covetousness — love of the “wages of unrighteousness” (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11) |
| v. 12 vs. v. 20 | Directive will vs. permissive will — God’s “yes” was judgment, not approval |
| The talking donkey (vv. 22–35) | A miraculous act of God showing the prophet more blind than his beast |
| Application | When God says “no,” seeking a “yes” from Him is a dangerous testing of God |
